## Analyzing K-12 AI education: A large language model study of classroom instruction on learning theories, pedagogy, tools, and AI literacy

### Di Wu, Meng Chen, Xu Chen [∗,](#computers-and-education-artiﬁcial-intelligence) Xing Liu _The_ _Faculty_ _of_ _Artiﬁcial_ _Intelligence_ _in_ _Education,_ _Central_ _China_ _Normal_ _University,_ _Wuhan,_ _430079,_ _China_

### A R T I C L E I N F O A B S T R A C T

### _Keywords:_ There is growing recognition among researchers and stakeholders about the signiﬁcant impact of artiﬁcial AI education intelligence (AI) technology on classroom instruction. As a crucial element in developing AI literacy, AI education Large language models in K-12 schools is increasingly gaining attention. However, most existing research on K-12 AI education relies on 

### PedagogicalAI literacy approaches experiential methodologies and suﬀers from a lack of quantitative analysis based on extensive classroom data, 

hindering a comprehensive depiction of AI education’s current state at these educational levels. To address this gap, this article employs the advanced semantic understanding capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to create an intelligent analysis framework that identiﬁes learning theories, pedagogical approaches, learning tools, and levels of AI literacy in AI classroom instruction. Compared with the results of manual analysis, analysis based on LLMs can achieve more than 90% consistency. Our ﬁndings, based on the analysis of 98 classroom instruction videos in central Chinese cities, reveal that current AI classroom instruction insuﬃciently foster AI literacy, with only 35.71% addressing higher-level skills such as evaluating and creating AI. AI ethics are even less commonly addressed, featured in just 5.1% of classroom instruction. We classiﬁed AI classroom instruction into three categories: conceptual (50%), heuristic (18.37%), and experimental (31.63%). Correlation analysis suggests a signiﬁcant relationship between the adoption of pedagogical approaches and the development of advanced AI literacy. Speciﬁcally, integrating Project-based/Problem-based learning (PBL) with Collaborative 

learning appears eﬀective in cultivating the capacity to evaluate and create AI.

revealed a collection of 14 educational theories and design models ap- plied in the development of AI learning tasks and pointed out the AI4K12 Big Ideas framework as the most prevalent AI knowledge framework. In recent years, there has been a surge in research on K-12 AI edu- cation. Empirical studies have explored various aspects of AI education implementation, from curriculum design to student outcomes. For in- stance, Chai et al. ([2021)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess)usedthe Positive Technological Development Framework to assess student learning on AI issues. Kim et al. ([2021b)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess) investigated the eﬀectiveness of AI education programs in developing computational thinking skills among K-12 students. Recent systematic reviews have shed light on the current state of AI in education. Sanusi et al. ([2023)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg)conducteda review of teaching and learning machine learning in educational settings, highlighting the growing interest in integrat- ing machine learning concepts into curricula. Their ﬁndings underscore the importance of developing appropriate pedagogical approaches for teaching machine learning across diﬀerent educational levels. Lee and Kwon ([2024)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess) revealed that various topics are covered in K-12 AI ed- ucation, including fundamental AI concepts, diﬀerent types of AI, AI applications, and ethical considerations related to AI. Su et al. ([2022)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg) examined 14 learning experiences in the Asian-Paciﬁc region, mapping AI tools, activities, educational models, and research outcomes. Li et al. ([(2024)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess) analyzed learning task design in 47 empirical studies on K-12 AI education, identifying four dimensions including theoretical foun- dations, learning contents, pedagogical approach, and assessment and outcomes.

Despite the growing body of research on AI education, signiﬁcant gaps remain. Most existing studies rely on qualitative methodologies or small-scale quantitative analyses, limiting our understanding of AI ed- ucation’s broader implementation and eﬀectiveness. There is a notable lack of data-driven analyses of actual classroom practices in AI educa- tion. Moreover, while individual studies have explored various aspects of AI education, few have attempted to integrate analyses of learning theories, pedagogical approaches, learning tools, and AI literacy out- comes within a single study. This integration is crucial for developing a comprehensive understanding of eﬀective AI education practices. The advent of LLMs presents a unique opportunity to address these research gaps. LLMs’ advanced natural language processing capabilities can be leveraged to analyze vast amounts of educational data, including class- room dialogues and instructional materials. This approach can provide insights into AI education practices at a scale and depth previously unattainable.

To address the limitations, this study employs LLMs to conduct a comprehensive, quantitative analysis of AI education in K-12 settings. By analyzing 98 AI classroom instructional videos, we seek to provide a data-driven understanding of current AI education practices and their eﬀectiveness in fostering AI literacy, aiming at contributing to the grow- ing body of knowledge on AI education, provide practical insights for educators and policymakers, and demonstrate the potential of LLMs as a tool for educational research and assessment.

2\. **Literature** **review**

### _2.1._ _LLMs_ _in_ _education_

LLMs hold signiﬁcant potential for enhancing teaching and learning (Dao et al., [2023)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess). They are applied in various educational areas, in- cluding automated assessment (Naismith et al.,[ 2023;](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg) Khayi et al.,[ 2021;](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess) Moore et al.,[ 2022)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg), personalized learning (Xiao et al.,[ 2023;](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg) Liang et al.,[ 2023)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess), and intelligent tutoring (Chen et al.,[ 2023;](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess) Hicke et al.,[ 2023;](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess) Tack & Piech,[ 2022)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg). For automated assessment, LLMs have been ﬁne- tuned to evaluate student responses and discourse coherence (Khayi et al., [2021;](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess) Moore et al., [2022;](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg) Naismith et al., [2023)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg). In content cre- ation, LLMs generate interactive materials like quizzes and multimedia resources to boost engagement (Chen & Wu, [2024)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess). For personalized learning, LLMs help develop eﬃcient student models and instructional exercises (Liang et al.,[ 2023;](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess) Xiao et al.,[ 2023)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg). In intelligent tutoring, 

LLMs are used to create conversational agents, question-answer assis- tants, and comprehensive tutoring systems with features like automated course planning (Tack & Piech, [2022;](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg) Hicke et al., [2023;](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess) Chen et al., [2023)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess). Although current research on LLMs in education does not ex- plicitly address instructional video analysis, LLMs’ ability to process multimodal data, including video, suggests their potential for this ap- plication (Summaira et al.,[ 2022)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg).

Some studies suggest that LLMs can replicate human-like reasoning and decision-making in classroom instruction (Whitehill & LoCasale- Crouch,[ 2024;](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg) Wang & Demszky,[ 2023)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg). Whitehill and LoCasale-Crouch ([2024)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg)foundthat LLMs’ analysis of classroom speech closely aligns with scores provided by human experts. Similarly, Wang and Demszky ([2023)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg)notedthat while ChatGPT generates relevant instructional feed- back, it often lacks originality and depth. Whitehill and LoCasale-Crouch ([2024)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg)alsodemonstrated that automating classroom instruction eval- uation using LLMs and Bag-of-Words models can oﬀer teachers more speciﬁc, frequent, and actionable feedback. Wang and Demszky ([2023)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg) further explored the use of generative AI as a tool to coach teachers in classroom instruction. Although these studies highlight the potential of LLMs in providing instructional feedback, they oﬀer limited insights into how teachers can design and strategically reﬁne their pedagogical approaches.

### _2.2._ _AI_ _education_ _in_ _K-12_ _settings_

AI education has gained prominence in 21st-century learning due to the pervasive inﬂuence of AI technologies in various aspects of life. Recognizing the importance of AI literacy across educational levels, Governments worldwide, including the United States, China, and Ger- many, have implemented national AI strategic plans (Laupichler et al., [2022;](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess) Ng et al., [2021a)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg). Several nations are actively working to ad- vance AI education in primary and secondary schools (Casal-Otero et al.,[ 2023)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess). In the United States, the AI4K12 program is a notable initia- tive to integrate AI into schools (Heintz,[ 2021)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess). In China, the Ministry of Education has incorporated AI into the mandatory secondary school curriculum (Ottenbreit-Leftwich et al.,[ 2021;](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg) Xiao & Song,[ 2021)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg). Singa- pore launched the “AI Singapore” project in 2018 to develop students’ AI capabilities (Su et al.,[ 2022)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg). South Korea planned to introduce AI education for all high school students in 2021 and expand it to younger grades by 2025 (Kim et al.,[ 2021a)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess).

AI literacy encompasses the competencies that enable individuals to critically evaluate AI technologies and leverage them for eﬀective com- munication and collaboration (Long & Magerko, [2020)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg). The term “AI literacy” emerged from researchers’ focus on preparing students for an AI-driven future (Wang & Cheng,[ 2021)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg). This concept entails the design and implementation of AI learning activities, tools, applications, and pedagogical models (Yim & Su,[ 2024)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg). Ng et al. ([2021b)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg) proposed four categories of AI literacy: (1) know and understand AI, (2) use and apply AI, (3) evaluate and create AI, and (4) AI ethics. Touretzky et al. ([2019)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg) identiﬁed ﬁve key components for K-12 students to learn about AI: per- ception, representation and reasoning, learning, natural interaction, and societal impact. Evaluating AI literacy in K-12 education is crucial. Gov- ernments and universities worldwide are collaborating with researchers, policymakers, software developers, and educators to develop curriculum guides, tools, pedagogies, content knowledge, and assessment methods. The goal is to equip K-12 learners with AI literacy skills (Ng et al.,[ 2021b;](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg) Payne & Journell,[ 2019)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg). However, developing, implementing, and scal- ing AI curricula presents signiﬁcant challenges. To address these, it is essential to establish a robust, evidence-based research foundation in AI education that can guide and inform the development of AI curric- ula (Wang & Lester,[ 2023)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg).

### _2.3._ _Characteristics_ _of_ _AI_ _classroom_ _instruction_ _in_ _K-12_ _settings_

### Three widely accepted learning theories—constructivism, cogni- tivism, and behaviorism—serve as foundational frameworks for teach-

ing and the development of AI curricula (GSE, [2023)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess). Constructivism emphasizes active engagement and the construction of knowledge by learners (McLeod,[ 2024)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg). Cognitivism focuses on the mental processes involved in learning, such as how information is perceived, processed, and stored (Main, [2022)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg). Behaviorism, on the other hand, centers on observable stimulus-response behaviors and largely disregards inter- nal mental processes like cognition and emotion (Krapﬂ,[ 2016)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess). These theories oﬀer diverse perspectives on curriculum design and teaching strategies, and their integration into classroom instruction can cater to varying learning needs.

Pedagogical approaches in AI education encompass a range of meth- ods, including direct instruction, interactive learning, project-based and problem-based learning, participatory learning, collaborative learn- ing, hands-on activities, game-based learning, inquiry-based learning, and design-oriented learning (Ng et al., [2023;](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg) Lee & Kwon, [2024)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess). Game-based learning, for instance, is an accessible way to introduce AI concepts to beginners with limited computer science backgrounds, helping to sustain their motivation (Long & Magerko, [2020;](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg) Ng et al.,[ 2021a,](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg) [2021b)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg). Some researchers advocate for hands-on activities through case studies to enhance understanding of AI concepts (Shamir & Levin,[ 2022;](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg) Vartiainen et al.,[ 2021)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg). In project-based learning, the emphasis is on contextualized, real-world problem-solving (Vartiainen et al.,[ 2021)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg). While there are pedagogical guidelines for fostering AI lit- eracy in students (ISTE,[ 2022;](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess) UNESCO,[ 2021;](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg) AI4K12,[ 2019)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess), current research often relies on case studies to identify teaching methods used in classrooms, oﬀering a limited perspective that does not account for the potential impact of integrating multiple pedagogical approaches. Educators can select from a variety of AI learning tools based on learning objectives and tool functionalities. Lee and Kwon ([2024)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess) cat- egorizes these tools into three groups: programming languages and environments, machine learning and AI platforms, and educational plat- forms and provisioning, which include tools such as Scratch, Scikit- Learn, and School-Book. When choosing or developing AI tools, edu- cators must consider factors such as age-appropriateness (Lee & Kwon, [2024)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess) and alignment with the content being taught. It is also crucial for educators to regularly assess the eﬀectiveness of these tools in achieving instructional goals and make necessary adjustments based on feedback. Thoughtful integration of these tools can enhance teaching and learning outcomes.

Regarding AI learning outcomes, research has primarily focused on areas such as AI knowledge acquisition (Chiu et al.,[ 2022;](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess) Aung et al., [2022)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess), skills and performance related to AI (Park & Kwon,[ 2024;](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg) Shamir & Levin,[ 2021)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg), motivation and attitudes (Aung et al.,[ 2022;](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess) Chiu et al., [2022)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess), and social impact and career exploration (Lin et al.,[ 2022;](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess) Park & Kwon,[ 2024)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg). Notably, AI knowledge is often assessed alongside other critical skills, such as problem-solving (Park & Kwon,[ 2024)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg) and com- putational thinking (Shamir & Levin, [2021)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg). Although Lee and Kwon ([2024)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess) acknowledges the signiﬁcant contributions of these studies in en- hancing students’ AI literacy, no research has systematically evaluated classroom eﬀectiveness based on the four dimensions of AI literacy: un- derstanding AI, applying AI, evaluating and creating AI, and AI ethics (Ng et al.,[ 2021b)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg).

The integration of established learning theories, pedagogical ap- proaches, and learning tools is essential for developing students’ AI literacy through classroom implementation. According to Lee and Kwon ([2024)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess)’s systematic review, AI classroom instruction topics include (a) awareness of AI, (b) AI applications, and (c) future work in AI. However, existing research lacks a comprehensive, quantitative analysis of class- room teaching practices that encompass learning theories, pedagogical approaches, learning tools, and AI literacy. This gap hinders a thorough understanding of the current state of AI education.

3. **Research** **aims** **and** **questions**

### This study proposes a novel quantitative method for analyzing AI classroom instruction videos. The method involves converting class-

room instruction videos into teacher-student dialogues and using LLMs to analyze them from four perspectives: learning theories, pedagogical approaches, learning tools, and AI literacy. To our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst study that employs LLMs for the quantitative analysis of AI educa- tion in primary and secondary schools. This approach provides teachers, educational researchers, and administrators with an eﬃcient and intel- ligent means to explore a vast amount of AI classroom teaching data, facilitating the improvement of pedagogical approaches and the culti- vation of students’ higher-order AI literacy. The key research questions guiding this study are as follows:

### RQ1: To what degree are the results of LLM’s analysis of AI classroom instruction videos reliable?

### RQ2: Which learning theories, pedagogies approaches, and learning tools have been commonly used, and what are the outcomes of AI liter- acy in K-12 AI education?

### RQ3: What types of AI classroom instruction can be classiﬁed by integrating learning theories, pedagogical approaches, learning tools, and AI literacy?

4. **Methods**

To address the research questions posed, we devised two paths for analyzing the AI classroom instruction videos at both primary and sec- ondary levels: LLMs-based analysis and manual analysis. Drawing from the ﬁndings yielded by LLMs-based analyses, we extract and examine the salient characteristics inherent in the learning theories, pedagogical approaches, learning tools, and AI literacy associated with AI classroom instruction in K-12 settings, as shown in Fig. [1.](#tities-within-the-text-content-the-study-employs-nvidias-nemo)

Our study focuses on four independent variables: learning theories, pedagogical approaches, learning tools, and AI literacy. To analyze these variables, we developed a comprehensive Python-based program as our primary research tool. This program utilizes ﬀmpeg for Video-to-Speech conversion, OpenAI’s Whisper model for Speech-to-Text transcription, and NVIDIA’s Nemo (Nvidia,[ 2024)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg) for Text-to-Dialogue processing. The core analysis is performed using GPT-4 API provided by Microsoft Azure cloud services, which interprets the dialogue to extract information on our independent variables. We crafted specialized prompts to guide the LLM in analyzing these four independent variables. Our tool chain al- lows for systematic processing of multimodal classroom data, providing a robust framework for quantitative analysis of AI education practices.

### _4.1._ _Data_ _source_

Starting in 2020, China initiated a pilot program in select primary and secondary schools to introduce AI courses. A portion of these classes were comprehensively video recorded and subsequently shared as open educational resources. The dataset for this study is exclusively derived from AI classroom instruction videos from a central city in China, en- compassing a total of 98 videos, each conducted by various teachers. The duration of these videos varies, ranging from a minimum of 30 minutes to a maximum of 46 minutes.

The collection of 98 instructional videos is divided between primary and secondary schools, with 90 videos for primary schools and 8 for secondary schools. Speciﬁcally, the breakdown for primary schools in- cludes 6 videos for 3rd grade, 37 videos for 4th grade, and 46 videos for 5th grade. In contrast, secondary school features 1 video for 6th grade, 3 videos for 7th grade, and 1 video for 8th grade. The program is pre- dominantly focused on primary school, and the majority of the videos are concentrated in 4th and 5th grades. There are a total of 62 teach- ers, divided between primary and secondary schools, with 55 teachers for primary schools and 7 for secondary schools. Speciﬁcally, 3 teach- ers are for 3rd grade, 26 teachers for 4th grade, and 29 teachers for 5th grade. There is 1 teacher for 6th grade. Additionally, 3 teachers teach across both 4th and 5th grades, and 1 teacher teaches across both 5th and 6th grades.

_4.2.2._ _Analysis_ _of_ _class_ _dialogue_ _from_ _four_ _perspectives_ Considering the advanced text comprehension abilities and extensive knowledge across disciplines inherent in large language models, GPT- 4 is deployed to analyze classroom dialogue through a fourfold lens: learning theories, pedagogical approaches, learning tools, and students’ AI literacy. This analytical endeavor unfolds in three sequential stages: long text chunking, prompt construction, and instruction analysis.

•Longtext chunking. The upper token input threshold for GPT-4 stands at 8,192 tokens, yet the classroom dialogues in question extend between 10,000 and 19,000 tokens, surpassing the single input capacity of the model. To address this, a sentence-level text chunking algorithm has been designed. With the aid of the tiktoken package, this algorithm tallies tokens for individual sentences and segments the text into portions, each not exceeding 6,000 tokens. Consequently, the comprehensive classroom dialogue is systemati- cally segmented into 2 to 4 such chunks for processing. •Promptconstruction. The eﬀectiveness of large language model outputs hinges on well-crafted input prompts. For optimized AI classroom instruction analysis, prompt design is stratiﬁed across three critical dimensions. Firstly, the model’s role is articulated, casting it as an expert in AI education. Secondly, the model’s tasks are delineated, analyzing classroom dialogue from the viewpoints of learning theories, pedagogical approaches, learning tools, and AI literacy. Learning theories encompass Behaviorism, Cognitivism, and Constructivism. Pedagogical approaches span a variety that includes Direct instruction, Interactive learning, Experiential learn- ing, Project-based / Problem-based learning (PBL), Participatory learning, Collaborative learning, Hands-on only, Situated learning, Game-based learning, Inquiry-based learning, and Design-oriented learning. Learning tools are extended to both hardware and soft- ware resources. AI literacy is deﬁned as knowledge and understand AI, use and apply AI, evaluate and create AI and AI ethics. Finally, the desired format for the output is stipulated as JSON, to stream- line the integration with subsequent statistical analyses. Detailed prompt exemplars are systematically outlined in Appendix [A.](#ethical-approval)

- Classroom instruction analysis. The analysis is conducted using the GPT-4 model, which operates on carefully constructed prompts in step 2. At the beginning of the analysis process, the overarching prompts are introduced to the model. It is then explicitly commu- nicated that the classroom dialogue will be presented in segmented parts due to its length. Upon the sequential input of these parts, the model proceeds to the summarization and comprehensive analysis phase.

### _4.3._ _Manual_ _analysis_

The manual evaluation process is centered around the design of anal- ysis questionnaires and the manual quantitative analysis of the AI class- room instruction videos. Expertise in education was a prerequisite for the graduate students who were enlisted to scrutinize the AI classroom. Questionnaire Star served as the chosen platform for the aggregation of the responses.

- Analysis questionnaire design. The questionnaire is comprehen- sively constructed to explore four fundamental dimensions: learn- ing theory, pedagogical approaches, learning tools, and AI literacy. Formatted as multiple-choice questions, it comprises a set of ﬁve items, including one that speciﬁcally requests the name of the AI classroom. Every question enumerates all potential answers, ensur- ing alignment with the prompts of the large language model. For instance, within the learning theory category, the choices span Be- haviorism, Cognitivism, and Constructivism. Please see Appendix [B](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess) for the detailed questionnaire.

### •Manualquantitative analysis. Each AI instructional Video spans 40 minutes, making the manual analysis of each video quite time-

consuming. To address this, we employed a random sampling strat- egy, selecting 10 videos from AI classroom instruction videos. We enlisted the help of ﬁve volunteers, with each volunteer tasked with analyzing two videos. The process involved the volunteers viewing the instructional video for their assigned AI teaching before pro- ceeding to complete the corresponding evaluation questionnaire.

- Test-Retest reliability. It measures an instrument’s reliability by evaluating the consistency of participant responses to survey ques- tions with repeated testing (Smithies et al., [2024;](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg) Wisner et al., [2024;](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg) Bergman et al., [2024)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess). To ensure the reliability of our re- search design, we conducted a second evaluation of the classroom videos using a group of ﬁve volunteers. The overall correlation between the initial and subsequent measurements was 0.86, in- dicating high consistency. Speciﬁcally, we found correlations of 

0.87 for learning theory, 0.88 for teaching methods, a perfect 1.00 for learning tool selection, and 0.73 for AI literacy. These results demonstrate strong reliability across most categories, though the slightly lower correlation for AI literacy suggests potential areas for improvement in assessment criteria or evaluator training.

### _4.4._ _Comparison_ _of_ _two_ _paths_

Given that the outcomes derived from both LLMs-based analysis and manual analysis can be interpreted as a series of categorical choices, we utilize the Jaccard index to quantify the similarity between the re- sults obtained through these two methodologies. The computation of this measure is as follows.

_𝑆𝑖𝑚𝑖𝑙𝑎𝑟𝑖𝑡𝑦_=(_𝐿_ ∩ _𝑀_)∕(_𝐿_ ∪ _𝑀_) ∗ 100% (1)

_L_ denotes the set of results from the LLMs-based analysis, while _M_ sig- niﬁes the set emerging from the manual analysis. “_L_ ∩ _M_” denotes their intersection, and “_L_ ∪ _M_” represents their union. A higher Jaccard in- dex value is indicative of greater consistency between the ﬁndings of the two analytical approaches.

### _4.5._ _Further_ _exploration_ _of_ _analysis_ _results_

To delve deeper into the characteristics of AI classroom instruction in K-12 settings from four key perspectives—learning theories, peda- gogical approaches, learning tools, and AI literacy — we expanded our research to the classiﬁcation of AI classroom instruction and the inter- relationships among the four aspects. This comprehensive analysis was based on analysis results generated through LLMs. We treated the se- lection within each aspect as a separate dimension, resulting in a total of 19 distinct dimensions. Speciﬁcally, learning theories comprise 3 di- mensions, pedagogical approaches encompass 10 dimensions, learning tools are divided into 2 dimensions, and AI literacy is broken down into 4 dimensions. The analytical outcomes for 98 AI classroom instruction videos were organized into a 98 by 19 matrix. Entries in the matrix are binary, consisting of 0 sand 1 s;where a ‘1’ signiﬁes the implementa- tion of a particular approach or tool within that dimension, and a ‘0’ indicates non-implementation.

### _5.3._ _The_ _types_ _of_ _AI_ _classroom_ _instruction_

The AI classroom instruction videos analyzed have been categorized into three distinct types: Conceptual, Heuristic, and Experimental, each comprising 50%, 18.37%, and 31.63% of the total classroom instruction videos respectively. These categories exhibit signiﬁcant diﬀerences in their pedagogical approaches and focus on AI literacy as illustrated in Fig. [5.](#53-the-types-of-ai-classroom-instruction) Most of these three types of classroom instruction are based on constructivism. Below are the three types of classroom instruction from pedagogical approaches, AI literacy, and content focus.

1. Conceptual: This type of AI classroom instruction focuses on un- derstanding fundamental principles and theories. The teaching often emphasizes core AI concepts, enabling students to grasp the essential ideas and frameworks that underpin the ﬁeld.

- Pedagogical approaches: Direct instruction and participatory learn- ing are prevalent, promoting learning through discussion and en- gagement. For example, in the “Starting the Python journey” class- room, the teacher provides explanations about AI applications, such as logistics and medical uses, thereby giving information directly to 

theories, pedagogies approaches, learning tools, and AI literacy.

the students. In the “Into the Internet of Things” classroom, the teacher directly explains the working principle of smart devices such as XiaoAi speakers and smart doorbells.

•AILiteracy: There is less emphasis on enabling students to evalu- ate and create AI, focusing more on foundational knowledge. This type of classroom tends to prioritize understanding basic concepts and theories over the development of critical thinking and practi- cal skills necessary for AI innovation and application. Consequently, students may lack the competencies required to critically assess AI technologies and contribute to their development.

•ContentFocus: Conceptual instruction typically covers basic AI con- cepts and application scenarios. The topics such as “Into Big Data”, “Into the Internet of Things”, “Introducing Artiﬁcial Intelligence”, “Opening the Door of Wisdom”, “Starting the Python Journey” and “Journey to the Future” suggest an emphasis on broader under- standing rather than deep technical skills.

2. Heuristic: This type of AI classroom instruction encourages stu- dents to develop intuitive strategies and rules of thumb for tackling problems. Lessons often include case studies, and practical examples, that require students to apply their knowledge creatively and adaptively.

- Pedagogical Approaches: All heuristic classroom instruction em- ploys Inquiry-based learning and PBL, aiming to foster problem- solving skills and critical thinking. However, participatory learn- ing and experimental learning are used less frequently, indicating a focus on individual or small-group problem-solving rather than large-group discussions. For example, in the “Smart Navigation” classroom, the teacher fosters the spirit of inquiry by centering a 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig.** **6.** Three types of classroom

practical, real-world problem and prompting students to explore diﬀerent routes to their destination and choose the best one. •AILiteracy: The focus is on applying AI concepts to real-world prob- lems, but there may be less emphasis on developing collaborative skills due to the lower use of group-based methods. While students are encouraged to understand and utilize AI in practical contexts, the lack of emphasis on group activities may hinder the develop- ment of teamwork and communication skills, which are essential for collaborative innovation in AI.

•ContentFocus: These classroom instructions tend to concentrate on speciﬁc practical problems, such as “Smart Navigation”, “Explore the Sorting Robot”, “AI in Life”, “Exploring Face Recognition” and “The Secret of the Human Face”, with a medium granularity of knowledge points.

3. Experimental: This type of classroom instruction encourages stu- dents engage in designing, building, and testing AI models and appli- cations. The aim is to provide students with practical skills and direct experience in developing and implementing AI technologies.

- Pedagogical Approaches: Predominantly utilizing PBL, these class- room instructions encourage active and collaborative learning en- vironments. Direct instruction is less commonly used, supporting a more student-led approach. For instance, in the “Target Tracking - TheLittle Detective” classroom, the teacher designs an activity where students are tasked with creating a crime-tracking device. The students are divided into eight groups to collaboratively work on this task. Similarly, in the “Smart Trash Can (Lessons 1-4)” se- ries, the teacher engages students in brainstorming and discussing the issues associated with traditional trash cans and exploring how smart trash cans could address these problems.

•AILiteracy: There is a signiﬁcant emphasis on training students to both evaluate and create AI, indicating a higher level of cognitive skills development compared to the other types. This approach en- sures that students not only understand AI concepts but also apply them critically and innovatively to real-world scenarios. •ContentFocus: The classroom instruction often consists of a series of classroom instruction with a ﬁner granularity of knowledge points, suggesting a deeper dive into speciﬁc AI technologies or applica- tions.

The dendrogram produced from our hierarchical clustering analysis provides insightful revelations into the relationships between diﬀerent pedagogical approaches and their impact on AI literacy. As depicted in Fig. [6,](#61-comparison-of-llms-based-analysis-and-manual-analysis-on-ai-classroom-instruction) the distance value between “Project-based learning/Problem- based learning” and “Evaluate and create AI” is 5.20, the dendrogram clearly indicates a signiﬁcant association between PBL methods and the cultivation of capabilities to “evaluate and create AI.” However, pre- vious classiﬁcation results suggest that using PBL alone may not suﬃce for the promotion of higher-order AI literacy. Instead, when PBL is com- bined with Collaborative Learning, there is a notable improvement in developing advanced AI literacy skills. This combination likely oﬀers a richer, more interactive learning atmosphere that fosters deeper un- derstanding and skill development. The hierarchical relationship tree 

instruction’s characteristics analysis.

further supports these ﬁndings by showing that Collaborative Learning is linked closely with PBL and the “evaluate and create AI” capabilities at a higher hierarchical level. This alignment underscores the synergy between these methods and their collective impact on advancing AI lit- eracy. Additionally, the distance value between “Experiential learning” and “Hardware tools” is 5.20, it indicates that classroom instruction videos incorporating hardware tools tend to adopt Experimental Learn- ing methods. This combination is likely due to the hands-on nature of hardware tools.

6. **Discussion**

The integration of AI into K-12 education has gained signiﬁcant attention, with various countries and international organizations estab- lishing frameworks to guide AI course development. However, existing AI education research lacks data-driven analyses of classroom practices and comprehensive studies integrating learning theories, pedagogical approaches, tools, and AI literacy outcomes. This study addresses this gap by employing LLMs to construct an intelligent analysis framework, enabling the classiﬁcation of AI classroom instruction based on four key perspectives: learning theory, pedagogical approaches, learning tools, and AI literacy.

### _6.1._ _Comparison_ _of_ _LLMs-based_ _analysis_ _and_ _manual_ _analysis_ _on_ _AI_ _classroom_ _instruction_

To validate the eﬀectiveness of our LLM-based analysis framework, we conducted a comparative study between LLM-based analysis and tra- ditional manual analysis of AI classroom instruction. Our ﬁndings reveal a high degree of consistency between LLM-based and manual analyses across various dimensions of AI education. This aligns with recent re- search (Parker et al.,[ 2024)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg), which demonstrated that GPT-4 achieves human or near-human level performance across a range of tasks in an- alyzing education feedback surveys.

In terms of learning tools and learning theory analysis, the results of LLM-based analysis show a high degree of consistency with manual anal- ysis. The perfect 100% match in identifying learning tools demonstrates the LLM’s proﬁciency in recognizing and categorizing speciﬁc educa- tional resources mentioned in the course transcripts. This suggests that LLMs can be particularly eﬀective in tasks requiring the identiﬁcation of concrete, well-deﬁned elements within educational contexts. While there was strong concordance in identifying most pedagogical approaches, minor discrepancies were observed in 1-2 courses for Col- laborative Learning, PBL, and Experiential Learning. These diﬀerences likely stem from the LLM’s reliance on textual data alone, whereas man- ual analysis beneﬁted from visual cues in the video recordings. This limitation highlights the potential for enhancing LLM performance by incorporating multimodal data in future analyses.

The assessment of learning outcomes presented the greatest chal- lenge, with the LLM showing high accuracy in identifying ‘Knowledge and Understanding AI’ and ‘Using and Applying AI’, but occasionally missing ‘Evaluate and Create AI’ and ‘AI Ethics’ in 1-2 lessons. This dis- crepancy can be attributed to the complexity of inferring higher-order 

skills and ethical considerations from text alone and homophonic errors in speech-to-text conversion.

The high level of consistency between LLM-based and manual anal- yses in most areas supports the viability of using LLMs for large-scale analysis of educational content. This approach oﬀers signiﬁcant advan- tages in terms of eﬃciency and scalability, potentially allowing for more comprehensive and frequent assessments of AI education programs. However, the identiﬁed discrepancies also point to areas for improve- ment, such as integrating visual and auditory data alongside text to enhance the LLM’s ability and ﬁne-tuning LLMs on educational datasets.

### _6.2._ _Current_ _status_ _of_ _AI_ _classroom_ _instruction_ _in_ _k-12_ _settings_ _based_ _on_ _LLMs_ _analysis_

Our LLM-based analysis of AI classroom instruction in K-12 schools reveals a complex landscape that both aligns with recent research ﬁnd- ings and highlights signiﬁcant gaps in current AI education practices. This comprehensive examination provides crucial insights into the the- oretical underpinnings, pedagogical approaches, and content focus of existing AI curricula, addressing several key areas in the literature. The analysis categorized AI classroom instruction into three main types: conceptual (50%), heuristic (18.37%), and experimental (31.63%). This distribution basically aligns with recent studies on AI education content (Lee & Kwon,[ 2024)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess), reﬂecting a balanced approach between theoretical understanding and practical application. However, this balance may not be optimal for developing the full spectrum of AI literacy skills required in the rapidly evolving ﬁeld of artiﬁcial intelli- gence.

Conceptual instruction, focusing on broad AI concepts through direct instruction and participatory learning, provides a crucial foundation for AI understanding (Alonso, [2020)](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess). However, our ﬁndings suggest that this approach alone may be insuﬃcient for developing higher-order AI skills, highlighting a potential area for curriculum enhancement. Exper- imental instruction, emphasizing PBL and group collaboration, aligns with research demonstrating the positive impact of hands-on AI tools on students’ computational thinking and self-eﬃcacy (Shamir & Levin, [2022)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg). This approach shows promise in fostering higher-level AI lit- eracy but is currently underrepresented in the curriculum. Heuristic instruction, while employing inquiry-based and PBL approaches, lacks suﬃcient practical and collaborative elements. This gap presents an op- portunity for improvement, as collaborative learning has been shown to enhance AI literacy and motivation.

The analysis reveals a preference for traditional teaching methods over innovative approaches like situated learning and game-based learn- ing. There is the signiﬁcant deﬁciency in teaching high-level AI skills (evaluate and create AI), with only 35.71% of classroom instruction en- gaging in these areas. Our ﬁndings suggest that current approaches may not adequately support the development of higher-order AI skills, indi- cating a need for instructional redesign to address this shortfall. Perhaps most concerning is the signiﬁcant underrepresentation of AI ethics in classroom instruction, with only 5 out of 98 instances ad- dressing this critical area. This ﬁnding is particularly alarming given the growing emphasis on ethical AI. Researchers have emphasized the importance of developing an understanding of the risks, biases, and ben- eﬁts associated with AI as a crucial component of AI literacy (Jang et al.,[ 2022;](#pedagogical-approaches--interactive-learning-the-teacher-en--references-courages-students-to-engage-with-the-material-by-asking-them-to-guess) Monteith et al.,[ 2022)](#the-pedagogical-ability-of-abs-httpsdoiorg). The lack of focus on AI ethics in cur- rent instruction represents a critical gap between educational practices and the ethical considerations necessary for responsible AI development and use.

### _6.3._ _Directions_ _for_ _improving_ _AI_ _classroom_ _instruction_ _in_ _k-12_ _settings_

Our analysis of AI courses indicates signiﬁcant potential for enhance- ment in AI literacy, pedagogical strategies, and content design for AI education in primary and secondary schools.

The statistics analysis has highlighted two critical areas for enhanc- ing AI literacy in K-12 education: enhancing AI Ethics education and promoting advanced AI literacy. It is essential to integrate AI ethics more thoroughly across all AI courses, covering topics such as privacy, secu- rity risks, discrimination, and potential misuse of AI technologies. This integration will enable students to comprehend the broader implications of AI and encourage responsible usage. Additionally, there is a need to develop curriculum segments speciﬁcally designed to enhance students’ abilities to evaluate and creatively engage with AI. Such segments could involve advanced projects where students are tasked with designing AI solutions or critically analyzing existing AI systems.

Our correlation analysis indicates that combining PBL with Collabo- rative learning can eﬀectively develop higher-level AI skills. However, currently, less than 40% of teachers utilize these proven methods. Addi- tionally, innovative educational approaches like Situated Learning and Game-based Learning, despite their potential to boost engagement and contextual understanding, are rarely implemented. Future AI course in- struction should expand the use of eﬀective instructional strategies and incorporate both Situated and Game-Based Learning to enhance the ed- ucational experience.

The AI teaching in k-12 schools is often characterized by coarse- grained content and lacks a systematic structure, which impedes the development of advanced AI literacy. To rectify this, future AI education should focus on creating a more structured curriculum that progressively builds upon students’ knowledge and skills. This could entail a series of interconnected courses that gradually increase in complexity and depth, thereby fostering a robust and comprehensive understanding of AI. We recommend that future research initiatives focus on integrating multi-modal data sources to provide a more comprehensive understand- ing of AI classroom dynamics. Additionally, we propose that researchers design and implement extended research projects that track students’ AI literacy development from elementary through secondary education. These studies should aim to evaluate how diﬀerent instructional ap- proaches, particularly those combining collaborative learning and PBL, inﬂuence students’ AI knowledge acquisition, skill development, and ca- reer aspirations over time.

For curriculum writers, we recommend developing dedicated mod- ules that explore ethical implications of AI, including privacy concerns, potential biases, and societal impacts. These modules should be woven throughout the curriculum, progressively building students’ understand- ing of AI ethics as they advance in their studies. Furthermore, curriculum writers should focus on designing project-based units that challenge stu- dents to critically assess existing AI systems and create their own AI solutions.

We strongly recommend that teachers explore and implement in- structional strategies that integrate collaborative learning with PBL ap- proaches. This could involve designing group projects where students collaboratively tackle real-world AI challenges, fostering both teamwork skills and practical AI knowledge.

For policymakers, we recommend developing comprehensive AI edu- cation standards that explicitly require the integration of ethics through- out the curriculum. These standards should also emphasize the impor- tance of hands-on, project-based learning experiences that engage stu- dents in evaluating and creating AI solutions.

### _6.4._ _Limitations_

While our study employs LLMs to conduct a quantitative analysis of AI classroom instruction, the approach presents certain limitations. Our current analysis framework primarily relies on dialogue data from teacher-student interactions, lacking multi-modal data integration. This limitation can reduce the visibility of less dialogue-intensive peda- gogical approaches like Collaborative learning. Future research should explore ways to incorporate visual and other non-verbal data to provide a more comprehensive analysis of classroom dynamics.

A signiﬁcant limitation of our study is the analysis of pedagogical approaches based on single-lesson observations. This approach is par- ticularly problematic for comprehensive methodologies like PBL, which typically unfold over multiple lessons or entire course units. Our ﬁnding is that 42.86% of courses implemented in PBL may not accurately rep- resent the true prevalence of this methodology, as a single lesson may not capture the full implementation of PBL in a course. This limitation extends to other long-term teaching strategies that require sustained im- plementation across multiple sessions. Future research should consider longitudinal observations or analysis of full course syllabi to more accu- rately assess the use of complex teaching methodologies in AI education. The assessment of AI literacy development is based on observed teaching content and methods, which may not accurately reﬂect actual student outcomes. Future studies should incorporate direct measures of student learning and skill development to validate the eﬀectiveness of diﬀerent instructional approaches. Our study focused on publicly avail- able AI classroom instruction videos, which may not represent the full spectrum of AI education approaches globally. This limitation could introduce selection bias, potentially overrepresenting certain types of instruction or educational contexts.

The use of LLMs as the primary analytical tool may introduce bi- ases based on the training data and algorithms used. Future research should consider triangulating LLM analysis with other methodologies to enhance the robustness of ﬁndings. The statistical analyses conducted in this study are based on the LLM’s interpretation of classroom instruc- tion, which may not capture all nuances of human-led analysis. Further validation of these statistical outcomes through human expert review would strengthen the reliability of our ﬁndings.

Our analysis does not account for potential variations in student de- mographics, prior knowledge, or learning styles. This limitation could mask important diﬀerences in the eﬀectiveness of various instructional approaches for diﬀerent student populations. Additionally, all experi- mental data in this study are sourced from publicly available AI class- room instruction videos. This reliance on public data may introduce a bias towards instruction that is more likely to be recorded and shared, potentially excluding valuable insights from less visible educational con- texts.

7. **Conclusion**

This study addresses a critical gap in AI education research by de- veloping an innovative framework for analyzing classroom instruction using LLMs. Our approach provides a quantitative analysis of actual classroom data, moving beyond the limitations of previous research that primarily relied on literature reviews. Our ﬁndings reveal key insights into the current state of AI education in K-12 settings, identifying three distinct types of AI courses: conceptual, heuristic, and experimental, with conceptual courses being the most prevalent.

Our analysis indicates a signiﬁcant gap in training for advanced AI literacy skills, particularly in evaluating and creating AI systems. We also found a concerning underrepresentation of AI ethics in current cur- ricula. These ﬁndings underscore the need for more balanced AI curric- ula that incorporate ethics, advanced AI skills, and innovative teaching methods. Our study reveals that combining collaborative learning with PBL can eﬀectively develop higher-level AI skills, though PBL was im- plemented in less than half of the observed courses.

These insights have signiﬁcant implications for curriculum devel- opers, educators, and policymakers, emphasizing the need for more comprehensive and ethically grounded AI education. While our study provides valuable insights, we acknowledge its limitations, particularly in analyzing only processed teacher-student dialogue data and basing observations on single lessons.

Future research should address these limitations by integrating multi-modal large models for more comprehensive analysis and con- ducting longitudinal studies to better understand the long-term impact of AI education approaches. As AI continues to shape our world, ensur-

ing eﬀective AI literacy education for young learners remains crucial for preparing them for the challenges and opportunities of an AI-driven future. This study represents a signiﬁcant step forward in understand- ing and improving AI education, setting the stage for evidence-based enhancements to AI classroom instruction in K-12 schools.

“As an education expert in K-12 AI classroom instruction videos, you are conducting a systematic analysis of a given K-12 artiﬁcial in- telligence course from four dimensions: learning theory, pedagogical approaches, learning tools, and learning outcomes. In terms of learn- ing theory, it includes Behaviorism, Cognitivism, and Constructivism. Pedagogical approaches include Direct instruction, Interactive learn- ing, Experiential learning, Project-based learning/Problem-based learn- ing, Participatory learning, Collaborative learning, Hands-on only, Situ- ated learning, Game-based learning, Inquiry-based learning, and Design- oriented learning. Learning tools include Hardware tools and software applications. For example, smart fans and infrared sensors are hard- ware tools. Hardware tools do not consider common devices such as interactive whiteboards and large screens. Scratch and lab platforms are software applications. Learning outcomes encompass knowledge and understand AI, use and apply AI, valuate and create AI and AI ethics. Based on the above content, please analyze the learning theory, ped- agogical approaches, and learning tools employed in the given text, and identify the student abilities developed in the four dimensions of learning outcomes.
